T_{\bar t}(c_0,(a_n,b_n)_{n\ge1})=(c_0,(e^{-n^2\bar t}a_n,e^{-n^2\bar t}b_n)_{n\ge1}).

For each pair of rational line segments in the drawing certificate, compute the determinant of their direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate linear intersection equations and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Accept an intersection only when it is a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence, and at a crossing verify that the two branch direction vectors have nonzero determinant. Reject self-intersections and all unrecorded intersections. If any check fails, return `invalid-input`. Otherwise traverse the oriented knot once starting at $a_0$, label the maximal under-arcs $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, and introduce one symbol $x_i$ for the positive meridian of each $a_i$. For each crossing $v$, read its oriented over-tangent and positive in-plane normal. Let $a_s$ be the under-side from which that normal points and $a_t$ the side toward which it points, and read the over-arc $a_o$. Append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. Equivalently, if the incoming under-tangent follows that normal, append $x_o^{-1}x_{\rm in}x_ox_{\rm out}^{-1}$; otherwise append $x_ox_{\rm in}x_o^{-1}x_{\rm out}^{-1}$. The orientation of a positive meridian is fixed locally by requiring the knot tangent followed by the normal-disk orientation to give the ambient orientation. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and this one relator per crossing.

The input is a finite record $D$ and a designated starting under-arc $a_0$ of one oriented knot. First check that the vertex, edge, and segment lists are finite; that every vertex, bend, and point on an edge polyline has rational coordinates; and that each polyline has the prescribed incident endpoints. Before geometric tests, delete consecutive repeated coordinates from each polyline; reject an edge with no positive-length segment or a crossing with a zero-length incident ray. Check that every crossing has four incident half-edges, a recorded cyclic order and a pairing into alternating opposite branches, and one designated over-branch; every other vertex must be a valence-two bend. Check that edge orientations agree at bends and continue coherently through each paired branch, and that following these pairings and bends traces one oriented circle. If $a_0$ is not one of the resulting under-arcs, or any structural check fails, return invalid-input.

For every unordered pair of line segments, compute the determinant of their rational direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate intersection equations over $\mathbb{Q}$ and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Reject every self-intersection, every positive-length overlap, and every intersection except a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence. At each crossing, sort the four nonzero incident rays by half-plane and exact determinant comparisons; reject the input if two rays have the same direction, if this geometric cyclic order disagrees with the recorded order, or if the paired branches do not alternate. These checks are finite.

After validation, traverse the oriented knot once from $a_0$, label the maximal under-arcs $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, and introduce one symbol $x_i$ for the positive meridian of each $a_i$. At each crossing, let the outgoing over-half-edge be the ray in the direction of the oriented over-tangent. In the verified counterclockwise cyclic order, the under-half-edge immediately following it is the target side $a_t$; the other under-half-edge is the source side $a_s$. Read the over-arc $a_o$ and append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. This rule uses the positive in-plane normal, which points counterclockwise from the oriented over-tangent, and does not depend on the under-strand direction. The orientation of each positive meridian is fixed by requiring the oriented knot tangent followed by its normal-disk orientation to give the ambient orientation. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and one relator per crossing.

A **rack** is a set $R$ with a binary operation $*:R\times R\to R$ such
that for every $y\in R$ the right translation $R_y(x)=x*y$ is a bijection
and $(x*y)*z=(x*z)*(y*z)$ for all $x,y,z\in R$. A **quandle** is a rack
satisfying $x*x=x$ for every $x$. For either structure, write
$x\mathbin{\bar *}y=R_y^{-1}(x)$.

For a regular oriented link diagram $D$, let $A(D)$ be its finite set of
maximal under-arcs. Form the set of finite terms recursively: each symbol
$x_a$ for $a\in A(D)$ is a term, and if $s,t$ are terms then $s*t$ and
$s\mathbin{\bar *}t$ are terms. Let $\sim$ be the intersection of all
equivalence relations on these terms that are compatible with both operations
and contain the quandle identities: idempotency, right invertibility, and
right self-distributivity, together with the crossing relations.
At a crossing with source and target under-arcs $u,v$ and overarc $o$, the
crossing relation is $x_v=x_u*x_o$; reversing source and target gives the
equivalent relation with $\bar *$. The quotient term set $Q(D)$ is the
**diagram quandle**, or the diagram presentation of the **fundamental
quandle**. Its independence of diagram is proved in the Theorem.

For any quandle $Q$, its **adjoint group** $\operatorname{Adj}(Q)$ is the
group presentation with generators $e_q$ for all $q\in Q$ and relators
$e_{q*r}=e_r^{-1}e_qe_r$ for all $q,r\in Q$. A group presentation
$\langle X\mid S\rangle$ means the quotient of the free group on $X$ by the
normal closure of the relator words $S$.

The diagram presentation and the adjoint group are algebraic constructions;
this definition makes no completeness or knot-classification assertion.

In the InverseBench two-dimensional Navier–Stokes case, the spatial domain is the periodic square $(0,2\pi)^2$ (the flat torus). The velocity $u(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2$ is divergence-free, and its scalar vorticity is $w=\partial_1u_2-\partial_2u_1$. For viscosity $\nu>0$, forcing $f(x)$, and initial vorticity $w_0$, the forward model is

$$\partial_tw+u\cdot\nabla w=\nu\Delta w+f,\qquad \nabla\cdot u=0,\qquad w(\cdot,0)=w_0.$$

The reconstruction target is $z=w_0$; the observation is $y=PL(z)+n$, where $L$ is the numerical solution map from initial vorticity to vorticity at final time $T$, $P$ samples the final field, and $n$ is Gaussian measurement noise. In the InverseBench two-dimensional Navier–Stokes case, the spatial domain is the periodic square $(0,2\pi)^2$ (the flat torus). In the physical vorticity model, the periodic velocity $u(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2$ is divergence-free and its scalar curl is $\omega=\partial_1u_2-\partial_2u_1$. This curl has zero spatial mean. Taking the spatial mean of $u$ to be zero fixes the constant-velocity ambiguity. For viscosity $\nu>0$, forcing $f(x)=-4\cos(4x_2)$, and compatible initial curl $\omega_0$, the physical model is

$$\partial_t\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega=\nu\Delta\omega+f,\qquad \nabla\cdot u=0,\qquad \omega(\cdot,0)=\omega_0.$$

The released benchmark uses a finite-grid scalar state denoted $w$. Its pinned solver computes velocity by Fourier streamfunction derivatives, which select zero spatial mean velocity and ignore the constant Fourier mode of the scalar state. The nonlinear term uses a dealiased state with zero mode removed, while the time-update formula retains the original state's zero mode; the specified forcing also has zero mean. Thus the solver defines a scalar-state extension even when $\overline w\ne0$. One must not identify such an entire state with the curl of a periodic velocity. In the corresponding continuum mean-split convention, $w=\overline w+\omega$, $-\Delta\psi=\omega$, and $u=(\partial_2\psi,-\partial_1\psi)$; only $\omega=w-\overline w$ is the curl, and $\overline w$ is a conserved scalar offset. This convention explains the zero-mode distinction; it does not assert that the finite-grid dealiased scheme is an exact continuum solution or that the released dataset has been projected to zero mean.

The reconstruction target is the supplied dataset field $z=w_0$ used as initial state for the inversion solver; the observation is $y=PL(z)+n$, where $L$ is this numerical scalar-state solution map over the specified inversion horizon $T$, $P$ samples the final field, and $n$ is Gaussian measurement noise. The dataset-generation horizon is a separate five time units: §4.1 and Appendix B.5 report independent Gaussian seed fields $\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,(-\Delta+9I)^{-4})$, evolved under the stated forcing for five time units to produce the dataset of nontrivial initial fields. Accordingly, $z$ denotes the evolved field, not a claim that the inversion-input distribution remains Gaussian with the seed covariance. On the full periodic space the reported covariance gives the constant eigenmode variance $9^{-4}>0$; the paper does not specify a zero-mode projection for the seed law. The scalar-state implementation permits retaining that offset without asserting the incompatible identity $w=\nabla\times u$ for arbitrary seeds.

InverseBench uses a pseudo-spectral solver with adaptive time stepping; the reported setup has a $128\times128$ grid, Reynolds number $200$, $10{,}000$ training samples, one validation sample, and ten test samples. The paper reports black-box forward access without a closed-form gradient for this implementation; the one-validation/ten-test split is part of this empirical benchmark, not a population-level guarantee.
